claim: Chromatin assembly involves the combined action of ATP-dependent motor proteins and histone chaperones.
source: Chromatin assembly involves the combined action of ATP-dependent motor proteins and histone chaperones.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Motor proteins in chromatin assembly also function as chromatin remodeling factors.
source: Because motor proteins in chromatin assembly also function as chromatin remodeling factors, we investigated the relationship between ATP-driven chromatin assembly and chromatin remodeling in the generation of periodic nucleosome arrays.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Chromatin remodeling-defective Chd1 motor proteins are able to catalyze ATP-dependent chromatin assembly.
source: We found that chromatin remodeling-defective Chd1 motor proteins are able to catalyze ATP-dependent chromatin assembly.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Nucleosomes assembled by chromatin remodeling-defective Chd1 are not spaced in periodic arrays.
source: The resulting nucleosomes are not, however, spaced in periodic arrays.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Wild-type Chd1 can catalyze the conversion of randomly-distributed nucleosomes into periodic arrays.
source: Wild-type Chd1, but not chromatin remodeling-defective Chd1, can catalyze the conversion of randomly-distributed nucleosomes into periodic arrays.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Chromatin remodeling-defective Chd1 cannot catalyze the conversion of randomly-distributed nucleosomes into periodic arrays.
source: Wild-type Chd1, but not chromatin remodeling-defective Chd1, can catalyze the conversion of randomly-distributed nucleosomes into periodic arrays.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is a functional distinction between ATP-dependent nucleosome assembly and chromatin remodeling.
source: These results reveal a functional distinction between ATP-dependent nucleosome assembly and chromatin remodeling
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental results showing that assembly and remodeling can be separated.

claim: Chromatin assembly involves a two-step process where randomly-distributed nucleosomes are formed first by nucleosome assembly function of Chd1, then converted to regularly-spaced arrays by chromatin remodeling activity of Chd1.
source: and suggest a model for chromatin assembly in which randomly-distributed nucleosomes are formed by the nucleosome assembly function of Chd1, and then regularly-spaced nucleosome arrays are generated by the chromatin remodeling activity of Chd1.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings, representing an inference from the data.

claim: Nucleosome assembly was originally discovered by Worcel et al. to be an active ATP-driven process.
source: The assembly of nucleosomes is necessary for the regeneration of chromatin following DNA replication, transcription, and DNA repair, and is an active ATP-driven process, as originally discovered by Worcel et al. (Glikin et al., 1984; Ruberti and Worcel, 1986).
evidence: This statement cites prior work by Worcel et al.

claim: Nucleosome assembly is facilitated by the combined activities of ATP-dependent motor proteins and histone chaperones.
source: Nucleosome assembly is facilitated by the combined activities of ATP-dependent motor proteins (reviewed in Haushalter and Kadonaga, 2003; Lusser and Kadonaga, 2004) and histone chaperones (reviewed in Corpet and Almouzni, 2009; Campos and Reinberg, 2010; Das et al., 2010; Ransom et al., 2010; Avvakumov et al., 2011; Elsässer and D'Arcy, 2012; Burgess and Zhang, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to review articles.

claim: Histone chaperones initially deposit core histones onto DNA to form non-nucleosomal histone–DNA intermediates (prenucleosomes).
source: Histone chaperones initially deposit core histones onto DNA to form non-nucleosomal histone–DNA intermediates (prenucleosomes), which can then be converted into periodic arrays of canonical nucleosomes by ATP-driven motor proteins (Torigoe et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement cites prior work by Torigoe et al., 2011.

claim: Prenucleosomes can be converted into periodic arrays of canonical nucleosomes by ATP-driven motor proteins.
source: Histone chaperones initially deposit core histones onto DNA to form non-nucleosomal histone–DNA intermediates (prenucleosomes), which can then be converted into periodic arrays of canonical nucleosomes by ATP-driven motor proteins (Torigoe et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement cites prior work by Torigoe et al., 2011.

claim: ATP-dependent factors that participate in chromatin assembly include Chd1, ATRX, and several ISWI-containing complexes.
source: ATP-dependent factors that participate in chromatin assembly include Chd1 (chromo-ATPase/helicase-DNA-binding protein 1), ATRX (alpha thalassemia/mental retardation syndrome X-linked), and several ISWI (imitation switch)-containing complexes, such as ACF (ATP-utilizing chromatin assembly and remodeling factor), CHRAC (chromatin accessibility complex), RSF (remodeling and spacing factor), and ToRC (Toutatis-containing chromatin remodeling complex) (Ito et al., 1997; Varga-Weisz et al., 1997; Loyola et al., 2001; Lusser et al., 2005; Lewis et al., 2010; Emelyanov et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Motor proteins involved in chromatin assembly exhibit both chromatin assembly and remodeling activities.
source: These motor proteins exhibit both chromatin assembly and remodeling activities, and are members of the SNF2 (sucrose non-fermenting 2) protein family, which comprises the ATPases that are known to be involved in chromatin remodeling (reviewed in Clapier and Cairns, 2009; Flaus and Owen-Hughes, 2011; Hargreaves and Crabtree, 2011; Ryan and Owen-Hughes, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Motor proteins involved in chromatin assembly are members of the SNF2 protein family.
source: These motor proteins exhibit both chromatin assembly and remodeling activities, and are members of the SNF2 (sucrose non-fermenting 2) protein family, which comprises the ATPases that are known to be involved in chromatin remodeling (reviewed in Clapier and Cairns, 2009; Flaus and Owen-Hughes, 2011; Hargreaves and Crabtree, 2011; Ryan and Owen-Hughes, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Efficient chromatin assembly by Chd1, ACF, and ToRC requires both a histone chaperone (such as NAP1) and the motor protein.
source: With the Chd1, ACF, and ToRC motor proteins, it has been shown that efficient chromatin assembly requires both a histone chaperone (such as NAP1) and the motor protein (Ito et al., 1997, 1999; Lusser et al., 2005; Emelyanov et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Chd1, ACF, and ToRC motor proteins are not able to catalyze chromatin assembly in the absence of a histone chaperone.
source: Hence, the Chd1, ACF, and ToRC motor proteins are not able to catalyze chromatin assembly in the absence of a histone chaperone.
evidence: This is inferred from the previous statement about requiring both components.

claim: Mutant Chd1 proteins (Δ932–940 and W932A) are defective for chromatin remodeling activity yet retain substantial ATPase activity.
source: To determine whether nucleosome assembly requires the ability to reposition nucleosomes, we examined the properties of mutant Chd1 proteins that are defective for chromatin remodeling activity yet retain a substantial amount of their ATPase activity (Patel et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement cites prior work by Patel et al., 2011.

claim: yChd1 Δ932–940 and W932A exhibit substantial (~40% of wild-type) nucleosome-stimulated ATPase activity.
source: we analyzed two mutant versions of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Chd1 (yChd1) that exhibit substantial (∼40% of wild-type) nucleosome-stimulated ATPase activity but are nearly completely deficient (<0.1% of wild-type) in chromatin remodeling activity, as assessed by the nucleosome sliding assay (Patel et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement cites prior characterization by Patel et al., 2011.

claim: yChd1 Δ932–940 and W932A are nearly completely deficient (<0.1% of wild-type) in chromatin remodeling activity.
source: we analyzed two mutant versions of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Chd1 (yChd1) that exhibit substantial (∼40% of wild-type) nucleosome-stimulated ATPase activity but are nearly completely deficient (<0.1% of wild-type) in chromatin remodeling activity, as assessed by the nucleosome sliding assay (Patel et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement cites prior characterization by Patel et al., 2011.

claim: The Δ932–940 and W932A mutations of yChd1 block its ability to couple ATPase activity to nucleosome remodeling/sliding.
source: The Δ932–940 and W932A mutations of yChd1 block its ability to couple ATPase activity to nucleosome remodeling/sliding, but still allow for robust ATPase activity.
evidence: This is based on prior characterization cited from Patel et al., 2011.

claim: Deletions of more C-terminal regions of yChd1 (ranging from residues 939–1010) cause the near complete loss of the ATPase activity.
source: In contrast, deletions of more C-terminal regions of yChd1 (ranging from residues 939–1010) cause the near complete loss of the ATPase activity (Patel et al., 2011; Ryan et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement cites prior work by Patel et al., 2011 and Ryan et al., 2011.

claim: Mutant yChd1 proteins (Δ932–940 and W932A) can assemble nucleosomes in an ATP-dependent manner.
source: In these experiments, we observed that the mutant yChd1 proteins are able to assemble nucleosomes in an ATP-dependent manner (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the presence of AMP-PNP, chromatin assembly by mutant yChd1 proteins was not observed.
source: In the presence of adenylyl imidodiphosphate (AMP-PNP), a β-γ-non-hydrolyzable analog of ATP, chromatin assembly was not observed.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the chromatin assembly assays.

claim: The extent of nucleosome assembly by the mutant yChd1 proteins was about 65% of that of wild-type yChd1.
source: The extent of nucleosome assembly by the mutant proteins was about 65% of that of wild-type yChd1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Wild-type and mutant yChd1 proteins catalyze ATP-dependent formation of DNA fragments corresponding to the length of a core particle upon MNase digestion.
source: With the wild-type as well as the mutant yChd1 proteins, we observed the ATP-dependent formation of DNA fragments corresponding to the length of a core particle.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from MNase digestion analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In the absence of ATP, particularly with mutant yChd1 proteins, there were DNA fragments longer than those obtained in the presence of ATP.
source: However, in the absence of ATP, particularly with the mutant yChd1 proteins, there were DNA fragments that are longer than those obtained in the presence of ATP.
evidence: This is an observation from the MNase digestion data in Figure 1D.

claim: Wild-type and mutant yChd1 proteins exhibit ATP-dependent stimulation of the formation of core particles.
source: In this assay, we observed ATP-dependent stimulation of the formation of core particles by wild-type as well as mutant yChd1 proteins.
evidence: This is based on native nucleoprotein gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The initial rate of nucleosome assembly by yChd1 Δ932–940 was approximately 8.5% of the rate of wild-type yChd1.
source: To determine the relative rates of chromatin assembly by the wild-type and mutant yChd1 proteins, we performed kinetic analyses and found that the initial rates of nucleosome assembly by the Δ932–940 and W932A proteins were approximately 8.5% and 12% of the rate of wild-type yChd1 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is quantified from kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The initial rate of nucleosome assembly by yChd1 W932A was approximately 12% of the rate of wild-type yChd1.
source: To determine the relative rates of chromatin assembly by the wild-type and mutant yChd1 proteins, we performed kinetic analyses and found that the initial rates of nucleosome assembly by the Δ932–940 and W932A proteins were approximately 8.5% and 12% of the rate of wild-type yChd1 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is quantified from kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Chromatin-remodeling defective yChd1 proteins exhibit substantial ATP-driven nucleosome assembly activity (~10% of the rate of wild-type yChd1) that is at least 100-fold higher than their ATP-driven chromatin remodeling/sliding activity (<0.1% of wild-type yChd1).
source: Hence, the chromatin-remodeling defective yChd1 proteins exhibit substantial ATP-driven nucleosome assembly activity (∼10% of the rate of wild-type yChd1) that is at least 100-fold higher than their ATP-driven chromatin remodeling/sliding activity (<0.1% of wild-type yChd1).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison derived from the experimental data.

claim: ATP-dependent catalysis of nucleosome assembly appears to be a functionally distinct process from ATP-dependent remodeling of chromatin.
source: The properties of wild-type and mutant yChd1 proteins indicate that the ATP-dependent catalysis of nucleosome assembly appears to be a functionally distinct process from the ATP-dependent remodeling of chromatin.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data comparing assembly and remodeling activities.

claim: ATP-dependent chromatin assembly factors such as Chd1 are able to catalyze the formation of regularly-spaced nucleosome arrays.
source: Because ATP-dependent chromatin assembly factors such as Chd1 are able to catalyze the formation of regularly-spaced nucleosome arrays (e.g., Ito et al., 1997; Varga-Weisz et al., 1997; Loyola et al., 2001; Lusser et al., 2005; Lewis et al., 2010; Emelyanov et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Chromatin remodeling-defective yChd1 proteins are unable to generate periodic arrays of nucleosomes.
source: These experiments revealed that the chromatin remodeling-defective yChd1 proteins are unable to generate periodic arrays of nucleosomes (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on partial MNase digestion data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mutant yChd1 proteins are defective in the ATP-dependent formation of periodic nucleosome arrays.
source: As seen in Figure 4B, the mutant yChd1 proteins are defective in the ATP-dependent formation of periodic nucleosome arrays.
evidence: This is based on nucleosome spacing assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Wild-type yChd1 has strong ATP-dependent spacing activity.
source: For example, quantitation of the nucleosome spacing data in Figure 4B reveals that wild-type yChd1 has strong ATP-dependent spacing activity, whereas the mutant yChd1 proteins exhibit little or no spacing activity (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is quantified from nucleosome spacing assay data shown in Figures 4B and 4D.

claim: Mutant yChd1 proteins exhibit little or no spacing activity.
source: For example, quantitation of the nucleosome spacing data in Figure 4B reveals that wild-type yChd1 has strong ATP-dependent spacing activity, whereas the mutant yChd1 proteins exhibit little or no spacing activity (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is quantified from nucleosome spacing assay data shown in Figures 4B and 4D.

claim: The essentially complete absence of spacing activity in the mutant yChd1 proteins was observed at concentrations ranging from 2–120 nM.
source: The essentially complete absence of spacing activity in the mutant yChd1 proteins was further observed in experiments that were carried out with concentrations of yChd1 proteins ranging from 2–120 nM (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The periodicity of the partial MNase digestion array slightly decreases upon addition of Chd1 proteins in the presence of AMP-PNP.
source: Examination of the spacing index also reveals that the periodicity of the partial MNase digestion array slightly decreases upon addition of Chd1 proteins in the presence of AMP-PNP.
evidence: This is an observation from the spacing index analysis.

claim: The decrease in periodicity upon addition of Chd1 with AMP-PNP may be due to the blockage of MNase digestion by static nonproductive binding of the Chd1 to DNA.
source: This effect may be due to the blockage of MNase digestion by static nonproductive binding of the Chd1 to DNA.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed effect.

claim: Mutant yChd1 proteins are able to catalyze the ATP-dependent assembly of nucleosomes, but are not able to mediate the ATP-dependent formation of regularly-spaced nucleosomes.
source: Hence, the mutant yChd1 proteins are able to catalyze the ATP-dependent assembly of nucleosomes, but are not able to mediate the ATP-dependent formation of regularly-spaced nucleosomes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: dChd1 Δ1099–1107 is analogous to yChd1 Δ932–940.
source: Specifically, dChd1 Δ1099–1107 is analogous to yChd1 Δ932–940, and dChd1 W1099A is analogous to yChd1 W932A.
evidence: This is stated based on sequence alignment and structural homology.

claim: dChd1 W1099A is analogous to yChd1 W932A.
source: Specifically, dChd1 Δ1099–1107 is analogous to yChd1 Δ932–940, and dChd1 W1099A is analogous to yChd1 W932A.
evidence: This is stated based on sequence alignment and structural homology.

claim: The nucleosome-stimulated ATPase activities of the mutant dChd1 proteins are 37–38% of the wild-type activity.
source: Similar to that seen with the yChd1 proteins, the nucleosome-stimulated ATPase activities of the mutant dChd1 proteins are 37–38% of the wild-type activity, whereas the ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling activity of each of the mutant dChd1 proteins is about 2% of that of the wild-type protein (Table 1).
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling activity of each of the mutant dChd1 proteins is about 2% of that of the wild-type protein.
source: Similar to that seen with the yChd1 proteins, the nucleosome-stimulated ATPase activities of the mutant dChd1 proteins are 37–38% of the wild-type activity, whereas the ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling activity of each of the mutant dChd1 proteins is about 2% of that of the wild-type protein (Table 1).
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Chromatin remodeling-defective dChd1 proteins exhibit substantial (~65% of wild-type) ATP-dependent nucleosome assembly activity.
source: The chromatin remodeling-defective dChd1 proteins exhibit substantial (∼65% of wild-type) ATP-dependent nucleosome assembly activity, as measured by the DNA supercoiling assay (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Chromatin remodeling-defective dChd1 proteins are not able to convert naked DNA into periodic nucleosome arrays in chromatin assembly assays.
source: but are not able to convert naked DNA into periodic nucleosome arrays in chromatin assembly assays (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Chromatin remodeling-defective dChd1 proteins are not able to catalyze the ATP-dependent spacing of nucleosome.
source: or to catalyze the ATP-dependent spacing of nucleosome (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The functional distinction between nucleosome assembly and remodeling/sliding/spacing in Chd1 is conserved from yeast to Drosophila.
source: Nevertheless, it is evident that the functional distinction between nucleosome assembly and remodeling/sliding/spacing in Chd1 is conserved from yeast to Drosophila.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from comparing the yeast and Drosophila data.

claim: ATP-dependent chromatin assembly does not require chromatin remodeling activity.
source: The analysis of the mutant Chd1 proteins indicated that ATP-dependent chromatin assembly does not require chromatin remodeling activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of mutant Chd1 proteins.

claim: Purified hBrg1 protein is active for chromatin remodeling.
source: The purified hBrg1 protein is active for chromatin remodeling (e.g., Phelan et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement cites prior work by Phelan et al., 1999.

claim: Remodeling activity of yChd1 was comparable to that of hBrg1 over a range of concentrations.
source: By using the restriction enzyme accessibility assay for chromatin remodeling (e.g., as in Varga-Weisz et al., 1997; Boyer et al., 2000; Shen et al., 2000; Alexiadis and Kadonaga, 2002), we found that remodeling activity of yChd1 was comparable to that of hBrg1 over a range of concentrations (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: hBrg1 did not assemble chromatin under conditions in which efficient chromatin assembly was observed with the yChd1 control.
source: We then performed chromatin assembly reactions with the same concentrations of factors, and found that hBrg1 did not assemble chromatin under conditions in which efficient chromatin assembly was observed with the yChd1 control (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: hBrg1 caused a decrease in the supercoiling of DNA.
source: Moreover, the hBrg1 caused a decrease in the supercoiling of DNA, which may be related to the nucleosome disruption activity of the SWI/SNF complex (e.g., Kwon et al., 1994).
evidence: This is an observation from the chromatin assembly assay data in Figure 6B.

claim: The decrease in DNA supercoiling by hBrg1 may be related to the nucleosome disruption activity of the SWI/SNF complex.
source: Moreover, the hBrg1 caused a decrease in the supercoiling of DNA, which may be related to the nucleosome disruption activity of the SWI/SNF complex (e.g., Kwon et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation citing prior work by Kwon et al., 1994.

claim: ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling does not necessarily result in the formation of nucleosomes from histones, histone chaperone (NAP1), DNA, and ATP.
source: These results thus show that ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling does not necessarily result in the formation of nucleosomes from histones, histone chaperone (NAP1), DNA, and ATP.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the hBrg1 experiments.

claim: Two ATP-dependent processes are involved in the formation of periodic arrays of nucleosomes during chromatin assembly.
source: In the context of chromatin assembly, our findings suggest that two ATP-dependent processes are involved in the formation of periodic arrays of nucleosomes (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: An ATP-driven chromatin assembly activity generates randomly-distributed nucleosomes from histones, histone chaperone(s), and DNA, probably via a prenucleosome intermediate.
source: First, an ATP-driven chromatin assembly activity generates randomly-distributed nucleosomes from histones, histone chaperone(s), and DNA, probably via a prenucleosome intermediate (Torigoe et al., 2011).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model, citing prior work by Torigoe et al., 2011.

claim: Randomly-distributed nucleosomes are converted into periodic nucleosome arrays via an ATP-driven nucleosome spacing (remodeling) activity.
source: Then, the randomly-distributed nucleosomes are converted into periodic nucleosome arrays via an ATP-driven nucleosome spacing (remodeling) activity.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on experimental findings.

claim: The two processes of nucleosome assembly and spacing may occur concurrently with wild-type Chd1.
source: Although we depict the two processes separately, they may occur concurrently with wild-type Chd1.
evidence: This is a speculation about the temporal relationship of the two processes.

claim: Attractive forces between nucleosomes may be maximized when the nucleosomes are arranged and/or compacted in a periodic array.
source: The basis for the formation of periodic nucleosomes as the final product of chromatin assembly is not known, but it is possible that attractive forces between nucleosomes are maximized when the nucleosomes are arranged and/or compacted in a periodic array.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the formation of periodic arrays.

claim: The internucleosomal spacing may be influenced by the interaction of the factors with DNA.
source: In addition, the internucleosomal spacing may be influenced by the interaction of the factors with DNA.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about factors influencing spacing.

claim: The individual rates of nucleosome assembly and nucleosome spacing are faster than the overall rate of assembly of spaced nucleosomes.
source: We performed each of these processes under identical conditions (Figure 8), and found that the individual rates of nucleosome assembly and nucleosome spacing are indeed faster than the overall rate of assembly of spaced nucleosomes.
evidence: This is based on kinetic data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The chromatin assembly process depicted in Figure 7 is compatible with the kinetic data.
source: Hence, the chromatin assembly process depicted in Figure 7 is compatible with the kinetic data.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the model with kinetic data.

claim: A conserved functional distinction between ATP-dependent nucleosome assembly and ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling by Chd1 was observed.
source: In this study, we observed a conserved functional distinction between ATP-dependent nucleosome assembly and ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling by Chd1.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: The ATP-dependent assembly of nucleosomes by Chd1 occurs in the near complete absence of ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling.
source: Specifically, the ATP-dependent assembly of nucleosomes by Chd1 occurs in the near complete absence of ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: These findings revealed a level of specificity in the role of ATP-dependent motor proteins in chromatin assembly that had not been previously anticipated.
source: Hence, these findings revealed a level of specificity in the role of ATP-dependent motor proteins in chromatin assembly that had not been previously anticipated.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the significance of the findings.

claim: The ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling protein, human Brg1, does not assemble nucleosomes.
source: In addition, the ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling protein, human Brg1, does not assemble nucleosomes.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: This model for chromatin assembly should provide a useful framework for the analysis of the regeneration of nucleosomes during processes in the eukaryotic nucleus that involve the disassembly and reassembly of chromatin.
source: This model for chromatin assembly should provide a useful framework for the analysis of the regeneration of nucleosomes during the many processes in the eukaryotic nucleus that involve the disassembly and reassembly of chromatin.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential impact and utility of the proposed model.

claim: The nucleosome-stimulated ATPase activity of dChd1 W1099A is 38±3% of wild-type.
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The nucleosome-stimulated ATPase activity of dChd1 Δ1099–1107 is 37±3% of wild-type.
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The nucleosome sliding activity of dChd1 W1099A is 2.0±0.4% of wild-type.
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The nucleosome sliding activity of dChd1 Δ1099–1107 is 1.8±0.5% of wild-type.
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The nucleosome assembly is necessary for the regeneration of chromatin following DNA replication, transcription, and DNA repair.
source: The assembly of nucleosomes is necessary for the regeneration of chromatin following DNA replication, transcription, and DNA repair
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: The extent of nucleosome assembly was monitored by the DNA supercoiling assay, in which the change in the linking number of DNA that occurs upon formation of nucleosomes in the presence of topoisomerase I is observed.
source: The extent of nucleosome assembly was monitored by the DNA supercoiling assay, in which the change in the linking number of DNA that occurs upon formation of nucleosomes in the presence of topoisomerase I is observed (Germond et al., 1975; Simpson et al., 1985).
evidence: This describes the methodology used, citing prior work by Germond et al., 1975 and Simpson et al., 1985.

claim: The spacing index is calculated as (0.5)(P2 + P3) − V2, where P2 is the maximum of the peak corresponding to dinucleosomes, P3 is the maximum of the peak corresponding to trinucleosomes, and V2 is the minimum of the valley between these two peaks.
source: The spacing index was calculated by using the following equation: (0.5)(P2 + P3) − V2.
evidence: This describes the method for calculating the spacing index.

claim: The spacing index increases with the periodicity of the chromatin.
source: The spacing index increases with the periodicity of the chromatin, and can be used for the comparison of series of samples that are under identical electrophoretic conditions.
evidence: This describes the properties of the spacing index metric.

claim: D. melanogaster NAP1 and topoisomerase I were purified as described by Fyodorov and Kadonaga, 2003.
source: D. melanogaster NAP1 and topoisomerase I (ND432 N-terminally truncated form containing the catalytic domain) were purified as described (Fyodorov and Kadonaga, 2003).
evidence: This describes the source of purified proteins, citing prior work.

claim: Native D. melanogaster core histones were purified from embryos by the method of Fyodorov and Levenstein, 2002.
source: Native D. melanogaster core histones were purified from embryos by the method of Fyodorov and Levenstein (2002).
evidence: This describes the source of purified histones, citing prior work.

claim: Wild-type and mutant forms of truncated S. cerevisiae Chd1 (amino acids 118–1274) were synthesized in bacteria and purified as described by Patel et al., 2011.
source: Wild-type and mutant (internal deletion Δ932–940 and point mutant W932A) forms of truncated S. cerevisiae Chd1 (amino acids 118–1274), which possesses the core chromodomains, ATPase motor, and DNA-binding domain, were synthesized in bacteria and purified, as described (Patel et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the source of purified proteins, citing prior work.

claim: Human Brg1 was purified as described by Phelan et al., 1999.
source: Human Brg1 was purified as described previously (Phelan et al., 1999).
evidence: This describes the source of purified protein, citing prior work.

claim: Chromatin assembly reactions contained core histones (0.353 µg), NAP1 (1.4 µg), relaxed circular DNA plasmid (0.294 µg), ATP (3 mM), topoisomerase I (1 nM), and an ATP regeneration system in a final volume of 70 µl.
source: All reactions contained core histones (0.353 µg), NAP1 (1.4 µg), relaxed circular DNA plasmid (0.294 µg), ATP (3 mM), topoisomerase I (1 nM), and an ATP regeneration system (3 mM phosphoenolpyruvate, 20 U/µl pyruvate kinase) in a final volume of 70 µl.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions for chromatin assembly.

claim: Nucleosomes were reconstituted onto plasmid DNA by the salt-dialysis method and purified by sucrose gradient sedimentation for nucleosome spacing assays.
source: Nucleosomes were reconstituted onto plasmid DNA by the salt-dialysis method and purified by sucrose gradient sedimentation.
evidence: This describes the methodology for preparing substrates for spacing assays.

claim: Nucleosomes for sliding assays were reconstituted by the gradient salt dialysis method using S. cerevisiae core histones and a FAM-labeled 208 bp fragment with a 601 nucleosome positioning sequence at one end.
source: Nucleosomes were reconstituted by the gradient salt dialysis method by using S. cerevisiae core histones and a FAM-labeled 208 bp fragment with a 601 nucleosome positioning sequence at one end (Patel et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the methodology for preparing substrates for sliding assays, citing prior work.

claim: Sliding reactions monitor the Chd1-catalyzed movement of nucleosomes on a 208 bp DNA fragment.
source: Sliding reactions, which monitor the Chd1-catalyzed movement of nucleosomes on a 208 bp DNA fragment, were performed as previously described (Patel et al., 2011)
evidence: This describes what the sliding assay measures, citing prior work.

claim: ATPase rates were determined using an NADH-coupled assay as previously described by Patel et al., 2011.
source: ATPase rates were determined using an NADH-coupled assay as previously described (Patel et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the methodology for measuring ATPase activity, citing prior work.

claim: Restriction enzyme accessibility assays were performed as described by Alexiadis and Kadonaga, 2002 and Rattner et al., 2009.
source: Restriction enzyme accessibility assays were performed as described previously (Alexiadis and Kadonaga, 2002; Rattner et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the methodology for restriction enzyme accessibility assays, citing prior work.
